in camp one year and I said that that was sufficient justification dnd entitled him to consideration, and I endorsed his appointment as captain of this particular squadron. But, in regard to Dr. Pickel and Mr. T. R. Pickel I said that I did not consider that their military qualifications entitled them to the positions to which they were being appointed. I did not object to their being appointed to some positions. I do not know much about military matters, but I do know enough to believe that before a man had put upon him the responsibility of being officer in command of a squadron in a cavalry regiment he ought to have some military experience and some military training. Therefore, I objected to Dr. Pickel being appointed as major of that squadron. Other names and proposals were in the list that I saw. Amongst them was the proposal that a certain Mr. W. H. Russell should be appointed as major of the Stan-bridge squadron and, in the same squadron, appeared the name of Lieutenant Holland, V.C., of Montreal, not as major but as captain. Now, Mr. Russell is a well known Liberal of the county of Missisquoi. , I pointed out to Colonels Whitley and Smart- and took the initiative in doing so-that it would be more fitting that Lieutenant Holland should have command as major of that squadron as he was a gentleman holding the Victoria Cross and one with South African experience. I suggested that change and that the experienced military officer should be given the command of the squadron, even though it meant that a well known Liberal should be put in a subordinate position. Another name that I found in that list was Lieutenant Guy Carr, of Compton, a gentleman living outside the district but in the eastern townships. I said that I knew Captain Carr to be an old cavalry officer. He was a well known Conservative in the county of Compton, but I welcomed his name in the regiment, was delighted to see it there and so expressed myself.
May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fisher) when all this occurred V

On the occasion to which my hon. friend the Minister of Militia referred-the occasion when he asked Colonel Whitley and Colonel Smart to come here to discuss matters connected with the regiment. I explained that on opening my remarks. Another name was that of Surgeon Major Macdonald. He is a well known Conservative politician of my own county who has always consistently-as, according to his principles he ought-opposed me in my political campaign. I insisted to Colonels Whitley and Smai-t that Surgeon Major Macdonald was the right man to have the highest medical position in the regiment because I had known him for years as an enthusiastic militia man ; he Mr. FISHER.
had been in an infantry regiment and if he were willing to take a position in a cavalry regiment as medical officer, it was his due, and I hoped he would take it.
I think this fairly enough disposes of the question as to my general interference, and as to the position I have taken. I will sum up this-and I take the full responsibility of saying it-that this regiment was to be established in the eastern townships and I wanted it to be a credit to the eastern townships ; I wanted it to be a cavalry regiment of which all the people of the eastern townships would be proud. As much as possible, if men of the proper mili-try qualifications could be found in the eastern townships, I wanted it to be officered by eastern township men.
Not because I had any jealousy of outsiders, not because I objected to men coming from Montreal or elsewhere to command it; the eastern townships, but because I believed and I believe it still, that men who are of the people there, men who know the country, the conditions and the character of the people are more likely to succeed in recruiting the rank and file for a regiment in the eastern townships and more likely to make it a success. When I saw that Col. [DOT] Smart was appointed to the command of this regiment I recognized at once that, so far as I knew the militiamen of my district of the eastern townships, there was no man there qualified to take command of the newly organized cavalry, and I supposed that the man selected by Lord Dun-donald and Col. Whitley, the brigadier of that district, was a man properly qualified. There was no objection to Col. Smart holding command of this regiment. The only suggestion I did make was that any further appointments to that regiment should be made, as far as possible, from the people of the locality who had the proper military qualifications. I believe that in asking for and insisting on that I was doing what was in the best interests of any regiment in the militia of this country. I have now explained the only cases in which I have discussed political matters in this connection. I only discussed them because I found in a particular squadron a list of officers which appeared to have not only a political complexion but even a family complexion, and I warned these gentlemen who, not knowing the country, not knowing the individuals, not knowing the relationship in connection with these people, I believed innocently, were led by local people into doing a thing which if it had been allowed to go through would have been a fatal blow to the efficiency and the success of this regiment. Sir, I plead guilty to that much interference in the matter on the ground of politics. And if that much of such interference is not in the interest of the regiment and of the country, and if men who apparently may have been-I do

not say they were-carrying on these intrigues in regard to military appointments, these political intrigues to which Lord Dun-donald refers, had been permitted to carry through their proposal, instead of being an interference on behalf of Liberals, of which I am accused, it would have been a deliberate interference and political intrigue on the part of Conservatives for the purpose of making this regiment what the old regiments there were, a Tory preserve and a Tory organization. If that is political interference I plead guilty to it, because ,1 object to the Tories getting the advantage of intrigues in militia matters just as much as I would be ashamed to undertake any political intrigues in militia matters for the benefit of the Liberals. There is but one other matter to which I wish to refer. Lord Dun-donald's last communication to the House has been before me for only a few moments. I have only had the opportunity of hearing it read and of glancing over it/ but I mud correct several statements which are here contained in regard to myself. Lord Dundonald says .
I accordingly twice communicated with Mr. Fisher by telephone o.n two dates some distance apart, and made appointments with him in order that the reason for the obstruction might be explained. Mr. Fisher did not keep either of the appointments. I
I am speaking now from memory as I suppose Lord Dundonald was writing from memory. Lord" Dundonald did call me up on the telephone to discuss this question. When he began to discuss this, I suggested to him that I did not care to discuss such a matter over the telephone and that if he wished to talk the matter over with me I was at his disposal. I do not know that I am called upon to seek out Lord Dundonald and to get him to ask his permission to discuss these questions with him. I think that, if Lord Dundonald wished to discuss these matters with me, he might very easily have come to my office instead of calling me up by telephone, and have asked to have a few quiet minutes in my office to discuss this question. I intimated to him when he called me up on the telephone that it was impossible to discuss these matters over the telephone but that I was at Ms disposal if he wished to discuss them with me. On the second occasion Lord Dun-rlonald again called me up and again began . to discuss these questions. I cannot for the moment remember the full words of what he said. He is right in saying that he explained the urgency of completing the organization of the regiment without delay. I agreed with him. He also then went on to say that the trouble was one of political interference. I said I regretted if there was any political interference. I had in mind the list of officers I had seen. Lord Dundonald went on to discuss the question
with me, and I again said to him I did not care to discuss the questions over the telephone. Lord Dundonald then said to me :
I am responsible for the militia of Canada and I cannot be interfered with in this way.
Hear, hear, that is right.

These are just about the words he used. I said that nobody wished to interfere with him that I knew of. He went on again and repeated that political interference was blocking the completion of this organization.
So it was.

He again repeated that he was responsible for the militia for Canada.
I said then to Lord Dundonald:	' I beg
your pardon, Lord Dundonald, but I think that it is the government of Canada that is responsible for the militia of Canada and not you.' I also said that if I had done anything in this matter I had done it as a responsible minister of the government of Canada because I believed it was necessary to make this regiment as great a- success as possible. Those may not be the exact words but that is the exact substance of-what I said, and without in any way desiring to attribute motives or to put thoughts into Lord Dundonal's mind, 1 fear very much that that gentleman has been influenced by the information which I gave to him that I considered it was the government of Canada and not he who was responsible for the militia of the country.
Lord Dundonald goes on to say a number of things to which I shall not allude with regard to Mayor Pickel, &c., as I have already dealt with them. He however, then goes on to show clearly by a letter to Col. Pinault, that he was perfectly well aware of the fact that I had been requested by my colleague to sign this particular recommendation. He knew perfectly well that that list of officers, was to be gazetted with the understanding that that name should be striken out. And yet his words at the banquet of Montreal, I submit to any unprejudiced person, would lead the public to believe that I, the Minister of Agriculture, had taken a recommendation of my colleague the Mini-ter of Militia and had changed it on my own responsibility. Now, if Lord Dundonald had felt as he appears to have felt, if he had shown that courtesy and attention to etiquette which might reasonably have been expected from one gentleman to another, or if he had shown a little^ common sense, which he might perhaps have learned in his two years' sojourn in Ottawa, he would, instead of rushing into a public speech, have asked either the Minister of Militia or myself for an explanation in regard to these things before making misstatements and creating a wrong im-

pression in the public mind and amongst the officers who were present at that Montreal banquet.
Now, I have only further to say that I have Col. Smart's letter to Lord Dundonald. I do not wish to cast any reflection on Col. Smart. I do not wish to say anything derogatory of him as an officer but I do venture to say this, that the tenor of this letter is such as to create an impression on the mind of anybody who reads it or hears it read which is not consonant with the facts as they have occurred. I have in my office to day letters from Col. Smart and Col. Whitley in which they express their extreme satisfaction with the stand I took in regard to this regiment and with regard to these, matters. I have letters from both these gentlemen thanking me in profuse terms for the interest I have taken in the regiment and asking my co-operation. I have letters from both of these gentlemen thanking me for pushing on the question of the establishment of that regiment and especially letters from Col. Smart thanking me for putting through the order which Lord Dundonald complains of. I will just now show the House and the country how utterly unfounded are these statements of Lord Dundonald and Col. Smart himself
. when he refers, as he does in this letter, to the case in regard to Dr. Pickel. I will read again Col. Smart's letter to me of May 19, on which I acted, passed and signed the order and recommendation to council. Col. Smart in his letter of June 4, to Lord Dundonald says :
I, therefore, communicated with Dr. Pickel and explained to him that owing to a new regulation, objections were taken to the appointment of unqualified officers, to field officers rank, and asked bjm if he would be good enough to allow me to withdraw his name temporarily, to which he consented.
X would point out that Col. Smart and Lord Dundonald were actually proposing to name a gentleman who had no military expsrience of any kind whatever, who never had been associated in any way with military matters, to the position of field rank, not ail ordinary subaltern in a squadron or company, but to a position of field rank in which he would have command of a full squadron and be responsible for the men under him in every respect. He says also :
Your Lordship will observe that I have not withdrawn Dr. Pickel's name absolutely, and have kept the position of major in ' E ' squadron vacant in the hope that I may yet have Dr. Pickel appointed.
' Then, I have Col. Smart's letter to me ou which I acted and I took no official step until I had received this letter from Col. Smart. This letter is dated May 19th. I would say in regard to this letter that Col. Smart came to me early on the morning of that day in my office when we talked over

these matters. After that he went from my office to the Department of Militia and Defence to have his recommendation embodied in a report and put through having said that he would try to get that report to my office that afternoon to have it passed by council. It did not reach me however, until the next morning. Col. Smart went back to Montreal that night-May 19, and met Col. Whitley as he says :
Immediately on my return this evening I met Lieutenant-Colonel Whitley and discussed fully with him all matters in connection with our interview of to-day. Colonel Whitley was pleased to learn that everything was arranged satisfactorily and at his request I telephone! to Sweetsburg with a view of getting from Dr. Pickel his final answer as to whether or not it was his intention to remain in the squadron.
Co!. Smart says in his letter to Lord Dundonald :
Your Lordship will observe that I have not withdrawn Dr. Pickers name absolutely.
And yet he asked him for his final answer.
And got it

And got it.
In accordance therefore with Dr. Pickel's request I can now as commanding officer of the regiment request you to kindly make the change in the ' Gazette ' by leaving Dr. Pickel's came out.
I acted in this matter not as a partisan politician, but I acted as h friend of the regiment, as a i friend of the commanding officer who was asking me to do this, and I only signed the recommendation to council after I had received a letter from that gentleman telling me that Dr. Pickel had given his final answer as to his connection with the regiment and after the commanding officer himself asked me to strike his name out. I did that, not in my own position as Minister of Agriculture, but, as is common in connection with the affairs of government, acting for my colleague who had requested me to act for him.
Now, I do not think that there is anything further for me to say except this, Col. Smart says that he has kept that position open for Dr. Pickel. Col. Smart on several occasions asked me to make a recommendation of an officer to fill that position. ;i said that I did not know anybody in the district with sufficient military qualifications to fill it and that I would not recommend anybody until I had been able to find such a one.
Captain Gny Carr, a well known Conservative in Compton county had been for many years a cavalry officer in that county and when it was proposed that he should be exchanged into this regiment I thought he was a suitable man-to occupy the position of Major of the regiment. The only name that I suggested to take Dr. Pickel's place was that of a qualified military man

.who was a well-known Conservative. Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not think I need go any farther. I would not have taken up the time of the House this afternoon had the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) not brought up these extraordinary letters and had he not undertaken to make insinuations and to make attacks upon me personally. I leave myself to the judgment of the House and through the House to the judgment of the country as to whether I have done anything to interfere with the efficiency of the militia of Canada or anything which is not consonant with the dignity of a public man.

Mr. Speaker, if anything were required to justify the remarks which Lord Dundonald made in Montreal I would think it would be the very distinct admissions which the hon. the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) has made to-day. He has admitted the whole case distinctly and absolutely. There can be do doubt of that and strange to say in making that admission he has to a very considerable extent in regard to the facts set forth in Col. Smart's letter, made a statement in absolute contradiction of the statement which he has read to the House this afternoon. Let me remind the hon. gentleman what he then said :
This is a simple statement of the facts of the case, which-without referring in any way to the propriety of the General Officer Commanding discussing in public, official recommendations, without referring to the broad question of the propriety of an official of the government of Canada criticising the official action of a member of that government-absolutely disproves the charge that for political reasons I have undertaken to strike out a name which had been submitted to the Minister of Militia for appointment in the service.
That was the statement of the hon. gentleman as read to the House this afternoon. The remarks to which we have just listened are not at all consistent with another portion of his written statement which is as follows :
In regard to Lord Dundonald's general statement that I interfered with the organztation of the corps and with the names of other proposed officers of the corps as well as Dr. Piekel, let me say this : that the only grounds on which I made any suggestion with regard to the establishment of this corps were the immense importance of the appointment of leading officers with military qualifications who knew the country and the people of the eastern townships, the district where the corps was to be established; that I took no exception to anybody's appointment on political grounds alone, as evidenced by my recommendation aDd endorsement of many well known Conservatives ; that no one believes more thoroughly than I do that the first necessity on the recommendation of officers on the establishment of a new regiment is miliatry qualification.
The Minister of Agriculture distinctly admitted this afternoon, that because Dr. i'iekel was a Conservative and because he did not think it was desirable that so many Conservatives should ho officers of that regiment, he suggested, indeed insisted, upon the withdrawal of his name and absolutely refused to permit the organization of the regiment to be proceeded with unless Dr. i'lCKel's name was withdrawn. If the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture do not mean that, I would like to know what they do mean. Why should the Minister of Agriculture be concerned as to whether any man appointed by the commanding officer of this regiment, was a Liberal or a Conservative ? Surely we have partisan politics introduced into enough of the aspects of life in this country without having the Minister of Agriculture running around and interfering with that which does. not concern him, and of which he knows nothing ; interfering with the work of those who know ten thousand times more about it than he does, and insisting that the officers of this regiment shall have a particular political complexion. And, if you get qualified men to serve their King and country in a regiment of Canadian volunteers what difference is it whether they are Liberals or Conservatives.
Yon will observe, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Agriculture was anxious that men of proper military qualifications should be appointed, and he sets himself up as an expert against the men who are charged with organizing this regiment. These gentlemen were Colonel Smart, against whom there is no word of reproach so far as his capacity is concerned, and Lt.-Col. Whitley, who is described in this way in the memo, which the Minister of Miliia road :
I was aware that Lt.-Col. Whitley, one of the ablest and most efficient cavalry officers rn Canada had been consulted with reference to the organization of the proposed new cavalry regiment mentioned.
And now, from the letters which were read by the Minister of Agriculture we find that his recommendations were necessary to every appointment that was made. These military men, these officers of experience, were not to be allowed to pronounce upon the military qualifications of the gentlemen proposed as officers, but the Minister of Agriculture, an expert, so it seems, in military service, is to be allowed to interfere and to prevent these men from serving their King and their country. That is the position of the Minister of Agriculture before the House and the country to-day. Let me tell him, when he sees fit to make an attack In a sneering tone upon the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes) who has served his King and country with distinction not only in Canada but in South Africa; let me tell the Minister of Agriculture that



he had better bear in mind that he, and not the member for North Victoria is on trial before the country to-day.
The Minister of Agriculture has admitted the whole case. No comment is necessary. Lord Dundonald's remarks are absolutely justified by the Minister of Agriculture himself. The Minister of Agriculture wanted no appointments, so he says, that would be inimical to the interests of the regiment. Does he suppose that he is a better judge of what is inimical to the interests of the regiment than one of the best cavalry officers in Canada who was in consultation with the efficient officer selected to command this cavalry corps. The statement of the Minister of Agriculture this afternoon, fn which he admits this uncalled for interference, has absolutely justified every word that Lord Dundonald has uttered with regard to this unfortunate matter.
Has the Minister of Agriculture ventured to contradict the very distinct statements which have been made by Lt.-Col. Chas. A. Smart, who says :
I submitted the name ot Dr. F. H. Pickel, who is mayor ot the town ot Sweetsburg, and warden of the county of Missisquoi, to be major in command of ' E ' Squadron.
It does not require very much knowledge of military affairs to know that in the formation of a regiment of this kind, as you cannot get qualified military men you must get men of prominence, men who are willing to be qualified, men who are enthusiastic in the service and who are likely to make good officers after they have been duly qualified. These officers were selected by the men who are charged) by this country with the performance of that duty. Lt.-Col. Smart continues :
Dr. Pickel is a gentleman of means, can ride fairly well, and was quite willing to take the necessary time to qualify himself for the position of major.
Let me point out once more, that of the sixteen men selected for officers in this regiment only two were properly qualified, but Dr. Pickel who happened to be a Conservative, is the only man according to the Minister of Agriculture, to be debarred from entering the service of his King, because he has not the necessary military qualifications. Col. Smart has no objection to this letter being made public, and indeed Lord Dundonald states he has desired that it should be made public. He proceeds :
Mr. Fisher objected to him for no other reason than that he was a strong political opponent of his, and was quite determined to block the whole organization, unless Dr. Pickel's name was withdrawn.
The Minister of Agriculture has not put it in quite such strong terms as that, but he has practically admitted the same thing in Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
his last statement to the House, although, the first statement which he read was of an entirely different conplexion, Col. Smart continues :
This, I refused to do, as I had invited Dr. Pickel to come into the regiment, and told Mr. Fisher that some one else would have to be responsible for the withdrawal of Dr. Pickel's name. After my last visit to Ottawa I consulted with Colonel Whitley, and we came to the conclusion that unless we induced Dr. Pickel voluntarily to withdraw, the organization would be hung up indefinitely.
Now, this gentleman is stating the conclusion at which he arrived, after consultation with the officer above him, Lt.-Col. Whitley, who has been described by the Minister of Militia as one of the ablest and most efficient cavalry officers in Canada. After consulting with this gentleman, Lt.-Col. Smart came to the conclusion that the partisan interference of the Minister of Agriculture in the organization of this regiment, with which the Minister of Agriculture should not interfere at all, was of so serious a character, according to the deliberate opinion of these two gentlemen, that the whole organization would be stopped unless the name of Dr. Pickel was withdrawn. And my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture has the hardihood, has the courage to stand up in this House, and before the people of the country, and say, that in playing that part he played a part of which no public man in this country might be ashamed, a part indeed of which he declares himself proud. Col. Smart continues :
I, therefore, communicated with Dr. Pickel and explained to him that owing to a new regulation, objections were taken to the appointment of unqualified officers, to field officers rank, and asked him if he would be good enough to allow me to withdraw his name temporarily, to which he consented.
I would like to ask the Minister of Militia whether or not the officers senior to Dr. Pickel in the 13th Scottish Light Dragoons, are all militarily qualified, because that is very important.
I believe they are.
Is the minister able to state that as a fact ?

That is my belief. I think there is no doubt of it. I have not the whole record before me. 1 have only the particular ' Gazette ' which we are considering. But my belief is that they are all qualified.
Is Lt.-Col. Smart correct in stating that of sixteen officers of the 13th Scottish Light Dragoons, only two had the necessary military qualifications ?
Nine out of sixteen possessed military qualifications.
The necessary military qualifications for their rank ?

Some of them were taken from former regiments. Some of them were from regiments that had been disbanded, with the expectation that these officers would be utilized. Others were taken from regiments in the city of Montreal. Without any doubt about it at all, I state that nine out of the sixteen had military qualifications.

My hon. friend the Minister of Militia must not suppose for a moment that we do not understand the difference between his answer and what I am asking. I am asking whether more than two of these men possessed the military qualifications necessary for the rank to which they were appointed.

I will only say that the ' Gazette ' shows that an asterisk was placed by the General Officer Commanding opposite certain names, with the following note :-
As a special case, and will be asked to pass qualifying examination.
That asterisk appears opposite only five names, so far as I can observe. In addition to those five, however, there are appointed lieutenants provisionally, and they should be added to the five namely, T. R. Pickel, H. W. Reynolds, and T. F. Cotton. That would make eight. That is the exact condition of things revealed in the original ' Gazette, ' which I have here.

I do not know that my hon. friend the Minister of Militia has made it very plain to me yet. It is perfectly clear that a considerable number of the officers besides Dr. Pickel had not the military qualification necessary for their rank, and therefore that part of the objection of the Minister of Agriculture disappears entirely. Lord Dundonald has stated, and I have not understood the Minister of Militia to contradict him, that in the organization of a regiment of this kind, it is always necessary to take unqualified men, with the understanding that afterwards they shall become properly qualified. Lord Dundonald with regard to that has said this :
Dr. Picket was not qualified professionally as an officer ; indeed only two out of sixteen of the proposed officers for the 13th Scottish Light Dragoons were militarily qualified. It was impossible, as will be understood, to procure duly qualified officers, as the cavalry regiments in the eastern townships had been increased since May, 1903, from four squadrons, numbering 300 men and 26 officers, to twenty squadrons, numbering 1,600 men and 180 officers on the peace establishment ; and with a war establishment of some 2,700 men. All the gentlemen, however, in the list submitted, undertook to qua-1471
lify professionally after appointment In the usual manner. This course is customary, and has been forced upon us by the lack of qualified officers. It is a course which has always met with the approval of the Minister of Militia.
Therefore that part of the argument of the hon. the Minister of Agriculture absolutely fades away, and we are left with the bald fact that the only obstacle which stood in the way of Dr. Pickel's serving as an officer in this regiment was that he happened to entertain political opinions different from those entertained by the hon. the Minister of Agriculture. That is all there is about it, after the hon. minister's own statement and after the best consideration which we can give to the facts brought before the House. That conclusion absolutely justifies the statements of Lord Dundonald.
And here let me remark that whatever else we may say of Lord Dundonald, I think we all believe that he came to this country, and has remained in this country, inspired solely and absolutely with a sincere desire to advance and improve the militia service in Canada. I do not think he has had any other object or aim throughout his entire career, and I believe that those of the military men of Canada who have come in contact with him and have thus learned to appreciate and to honour him, will bear me out in that tribute. He is a man of simple, straightforward character, a thorough soldier in every respect; and I can well understand the irritation which he would feel, and from which he undoubtedly would suffer, when he found that the organization of a cavalry regiment in the eastern townships was being hung up and delayed, and stood in danger of being indefinitely postponed, simply for the reason that certain officers proposed to be appointed to that regiment did not entertain political views in harmony with those of my hon. friend the Minister of the Agriculture.
The government, however, adopted a rather curious mode of dealing with Lord Dundonald. From the statements which we have heard read in the House this afternoon, it is perfectly obvious that what must have been construed as an attack upon that officer was proposed to he made in the House to-day, without calling on Lord Dundonald for one word in his defence. That is the position in which the matter presents itself. If the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Militia proposed to read these statements in the House to-day, would it not have been a fair thing for them in the first place to have either called on Lord Dundonald for an explanation of the remarks he made in Montreal, or to have submitted to him a statement of the facts as they understood them to be, and to have asked from him any defence which he might desire to make? I would have thought that the fair and courteous course, but it was not the course that evidently was intended.

I will say in conclusion that while 1 regal'd this as a very regrettable incident, it will not be without benefit to the country, if, in the future, it will lead to the withdrawal of partisan interference in the appointment of officers of the militia, whether that interference may come from the government now in power or may be sought to be applied by any government which may come into power in the future. We do not want political interference in military matters in Canada. The people pay a considerable amount for the military service of this country ; they are willing to pay that amount for an efficient military service; but we do not want that service to deteriorate or become inefficient by reason of party politics entering into -it in any way. We have had this afternoon a confession which indicates that party politics has been entering into it for some time past, on the part of the Minister of Agriculture at any rate.
I trust that there will be an end to that, and that the Minister of Militia will see fit to confide solely to officers who are experienced and capable, the organization of such regiments as this without considering, at the instance of the Minister of Agriculture or any one else, whether the gentlemen sought to be appointed are Conservatives or Liberals in their political opinions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The occasion of this debate Mr. Speaker, is the unfortunate-I shall not characterize it to-day by any other term-speech which was delivered some few days ago by Lord Dundonald at a banquet. After the explanations we have had from my hon. colleagues, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) and Militia (Sir Frederick Borden), and also on behalf of Lord Dundonald by my hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes), I think it preferable at this moment not to push further a discussion of the consequences which may flow from Lord Dundonald's remarks. Not that I should have any hesitation in my own mind, or that there should be any hesitation in the mind of anybody, but it is preferable, in a matter of this gravity, that we should proceed with prudence and deliberation. Having said that much regarding the speech of Lord Dundonald, I may be permitted to say a word of his methods in organizing the militia, in so far as they are revealed by the incidents which have taken place in connection with the organization of the 13th Light Scottish Dragoons. Lord Dundonald is certainly-I am willing to give him every credit in that respect-endowed with good motives. No one who knows him can question that. He bears a very honourable name, as was said by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) a moment ago, a name made famous by his forebears in British history, and to the lustre of which he has added himself by his own services in South Africa and

elsewhere. I have no desire in the slightest degree to reflect upon him as a soldier, but perhaps I may not be offensive if I say that it is not the first time that a good soldier may have lacked discretion. Lord Dundonald, in his position, is charged with the organization of the militia, but he must take counsel here when organizing a regiment. He is a foreigner-no-
No, no.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I had withdrawn the expression before hon. gentlemen interrupted. He is not a foreigner, but he is a stranger.
No.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, he does not know the people of the eastern townships, where these light dragoons are to be enlisted.' I doubt if he ever was in the town of Sweetsburg, or in the county of Brome, or the county of Missisquoi, or, if he has been in any of these places, it could only have been for a very short period, when passing through. It was advisable that a regiment should be recruited in those districts, but in what way ? If this regiment of 13th Scottish Light Dragoons was to be organized and recruited from the counties of Brome and Missisquoi, how could Lord Dundonald possibly know personally who should officer it ? How could he know what officers should be appointed ? Perhaps he knew Ool. Smart, but Col. Smart himself was from Montreal, and he had to go to the counties and get there his information from somebody. He had to get information from parties in and around Sweetsburg and the other towns in the counties of Missisquoi and Brome. Well, it is evident that Col. Smart happened to fall into the hands of certain parties who represented rather a small family compact. The list he made was composed almost exclusively of gentlemen connected with the Conservative party. My hon. friend said a moment ago that in militia matters there should be no politics, and in this I heartily agree, but it so happens that this regiment was to be officered almost exclusively by Conservative politicians. It is no harm to be a Conservative. It may be a mistake, but I do not count it a sin. But I submit to my hon. friends on the other side, is it not proper that whenever a regiment is organized in any part of the country, it should be officered as far as possible from both parties ? I do not know how things are now, but once upon a time, when I was in the militia myself, there was a battalion organized, with which I was connected, and in organizng it, the man who was our colonel went and consulted everybody. He consulted men who could not take any part in the organization, but whose advice was valuable. But in the present instance, it so happens that there is a gentleman in the eastern townships who is connected with politics and holds a position of some respectability in that part of the country, I refer to my

462U
hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture. Was his position to be considered a bar to his offering any advice ? Was he to be precluded from expressing an opinion simply because he happened to be Minister of Agriculture ? Had he not as much right to give advice in the matter as Col. Pickel and the others about Sherbrooke, or in the counties of Missisquoi and Brome, who hap-jiened to be consulted ? Was my hon. friend, simply because he happened to be Minister of Agriculture, bound to say :	it
is all wrong, you have chosen none hut Conservative politicians to be officers of the regiment, but I cannot say a word about it ? If we are all in agreement on this principle that volunteer associations should not be political preserves, if we all agreed that politics should be kept out of them, I think that my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture ought to be commended for having pointed out to the general that he was making a mistake in choosing nearly all his men of the one stripe and so few of the other ? That is all my hon. friend did. He wrote to the General Officer Commanding that there were in that regiment too many of one stripe and not sufficient of the other. He went over to the militia office and had a conference with the Minister of Militia and Cols. Whitley and -Smart. Together they discussed the personnel of the staff. My hon. friend made some representations, and it seems to me that the representations he made were in the best interests of the force and should have been accepted. As a matter of fact they were accepted at that conference, but unfortunateljr Lord Dundonald came to the conclusion that having signed a list of names recommended to him-a list probably of men about whom he knew nothing-that list was as sacred as the laws of the Medes and Persians and could not he interfered with-that even the Minister of Agriculture, acting for the Minister of Militia,-which is not denied by Lord Dundonald-could not have a word to say, hut that the list had to be accepted simply because it was signed by Lord Dundonald.
My hon. friend is not doing Lord Dundonald justice ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In what way?

He never made any objection to the Minister of Militia acting or to any one acting for him. What he objected to was the Minister of Agriculture going to the officers who were organizing that regiment under him and interfering with them in the duties they were performing under his directions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I beg my hon. friend's pardon. Here is the speech of Lord Dundonald. He said, would you believe it gentlemen, I sent an order to the cabinet and that order was interfered with. Here are his very words :
A most flagrant Instance of political interference hg.s recently come before me in connection jvith the appointment of officers in the new eastern township cavalry regiment, the Scottish Light Dragoons.
The commanding officers of the corp had been selected because of their apparent fitness from a military point of view. The names reached me and were sent to council and gentlemen, what do you think happened ? The list having my approval

' My approval '



was returned with the name of one officer stricken out and initialled by the Minister of Agriculture.
And, in justice to the Minister of Agriculture it should be said that it was initialled by him acting for the Minister of Militia, as was well known by Lord Dundonald. Under these circumstances, I ask my hon. friend if I am doing any injustice to Lord Dundonald when I say that he wanted to have his recommendation to council, the last word to be said, and minister and council simply to bow and accept his recommendation ?

I say, yes, because the Prime Minister has left out of account the letter from Lieut.-Col. Smart which was before Lord Dundonald before he made these remarks, in which Lieut.-Col. Smart said that" the Minister of Agriculture had interfered with him on political grounds.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And at that very moment the Minister of Agriculture, who was acting for the Minister of Militia had the letter of Lieut.-Col. Smart begging him to leave off the name of Dr. Pickel. Sir, we are not accustomed-I give_ all credit to Lord Dundonald for good motives __but we are not accustomed to be dragooned in this country. Lord Dundonald, with all the respect I have for him, must learn that this is a responsible government and that when he sends a recommendation to council, it is the right-it is the right, I say notwithstanding what anybody may say to the contrary-of the minister in charge of the department, if he does not approve of the recommendation to strike out any name.
May I ask the right hon. Prime Minister a question ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

Will he or will the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Militia deny that this name was struck off while the Minister of Militia was present with the Minister of Agriculture, before the recommendation was sent to council. If he does, all I can say is that we can prove to the contrary.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What does that prove ?
It proves that the Minister of Agriculture had interfered before.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It was corrected by the Minister of Agriculture, acting for the Minister of Militia and approved by the council.

Yes, but it was changed before that.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, It was not changed before that time. I do not wish to pursue this discussion further. I merely wish to vindicate the course of my hon. friend (Mr. Fisher). Lord Dundonald, or whoever commands the militia in Canada will commit the greatest of mistakes if, when appointing officers to the mifltia in parts of the country of which he knows nothing, appointments concerning which he must take the recommendation of somebody, if he does not take advice not only from one side but from both sides of politics on these matters.

I regret, as all must regret, the incident that has come before us to-day ; but I regret still more the evident joy with which supporters of the government hailed it as giving them a chance to get rid of a man who has been so strong to resent the interference of .politicians in appointments in the militia. There is no explanation wanted from any one as to the position the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) took in this matter. He interfered for a political purpose, according to his own statement. If he cannot see that it was a political motive and nothing else that influenced his action, then he cannot see what every one else in the House can see. The Prime Minister made a statement that seems to me rather extraordinary. He stated, as a reason for the interference of the Minister of Agriculture, who happens to live in the district where the corps was being organized, that the General Officer Commanding, Lord Dundonald, did not know the people and did not know the country. If that is to be the ground for taking out of the hands of the General Officer Commanding the selection of those to fill these appointments, then it means that in every locality where the General Officer Commanding is not perfectly familiar with the people and the country the member of parliament who may represent that section is, for the time being, to be the Minister of Militia so far as that district is concerned. That is what the Prime Minister tells us in so many words. Surelv that is a condition of affairs which could not be allowed, and I am sure the Prime Minister did not mean to convey the meaning that his words conveyed to me, and I think must have conveyed to everybody who listened to him. Any officer commanding the militia has a difficult position to fill He ought, I think, to receive all the cour- 1
Sir WILFRID LAURIE!
tesy and all the help possible from his minister and from all the members of the government. I think, from the correspondence and from the admissions that the Minister of Agriculture has made, that Lord Dundonald was thoroughly right in being indignant at the way he was treated. I think that no man with knowledge of his profession and proper regard for his own dignity could do other than resent the treatment the Minister of Agriculture meted out to Lord Dundonald in connection with this matter. Evidently it is not the only case which has aroused this feeling on the part of Lord Dundonald. He came here as an eminent soldier and he has won the confidence, I believe, of every volunteer in the country-certainly of every one whose opinions I have heard expressed. He is looked up to with the greatest respect, and all have anticipated the very best results from the improvements he has made. I regret very, very sincerely that this incident has happened. I regret still more the manner in which it has been treated by the members on the other side of the House. They seem to have a feeling of delight that Lord Dundonald has got into a scrape and that they might be relieved from his continued occupancy of a position he has filled with such credit.

I do not wish to prolong this debate which I think has gone a little too far. I must say I was rather surprised at the turn the debate took from the beginning. I did not expect that the Minister of Agriculture would be here 'to defend his case. To me the case was a simpler one than that-it was the case of an official of the government under the authority of the ministers of the Crown having made a public speech in which he had spoken in what may be called, mildlv, rather uncalled for terms of one of the members of the government of which he is the servant. I think it is well that we should understand exactly the point at Issue, not only before the House, but before the country. That point is whether the General Officer Commanding the militia of Canada is a servant of the government or not. If he is not a servant of the government, I quite accept the conclusion of hon. genuemen opposite and say that he should not be interfered with by politicians. But, if it is acknowledged, as I always thought it rvas acknowledged, that he is a servant of the government, that he is appointed and paid by the government and therefore must report to the minister-who is responsible to the House-before stating anything to the country, then, I think the course of Lord Dundonald is absolutely indefensible. Instead of being the case of Lord Dundonald against Mr. Fisher it is simply the case of a servant of the government who has been speaking in public and saying things he should not say. Lord Dundonald has thought proper to choose the hon. member

for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) to plead his case here to-day. If Lord Dundonald is a servant of the Crown, how can it for a moment be entertained that it is a proper thing for a servant of the government to ask an independent member of parliament, whether Liberal or Conservative, to plead his case against one of the ministers of the government of which he is a servant ? So I would now ask the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) who has constituted himself a warm defender of Lord Dundonald, whether he considers the General Officer Commanding the militia as a servant of the Crown just as any other deputy minister of the Crown is ?

I think if my hon. friend asks the Minister of Militia and the First Minister he will find that when the Minister of Militia and the First Minister and the whole outfit were crawling before the General Officer Commanding it was I who taught the people of this country that the General Officer Commanding is a servant of the people of this country.
Mr. BOtIRASSA. Then I think we have a judgment from the counsel, not of the prosecutor but of the accused. The hon. gentleman has been standing up here trying to justify the speech that was made by Lord Dundonald at Montreal, trying to justify the accusations brought by Lord Dun: donald against the Minister of Agriculture, and now he is stating before the House that he knows and acknowledges that Lord Dundonald is a servant of the Crown. Suppose the Deputy Minister of Public Works should make a speech in Montreal and say : ' X want to have a wharf built at Montreal or Quebec, in a certain way, but the Minister of Militia interfered and knowing nothing of public works has forced me to change my plans. It is a danger for the future of public works in Canada that a minister of the Crown should interfere with the prerogatives of the Deputy Minister of Public Works.' What would the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes), what would the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) say ? That is the whole question in a nutshell. I am not going to challenge the opinions of Lord Dundonald as far as military matters are concerned. I quite admit that he has a high reputation and no doubt he deserves it. But, it seems that Lord Dundonald and the other gentlemen who have been General Officers Commanding on coming to this country have never realized that they were servants of the government and that they were bound to make their suggestions to the Minister of Militia and through the Minister of Militia to the parliament of Canada. If a General Officer Commanding, Lord Dundonald, or General Hutton or any one else, thinks that the policy pursued by the Minister of Militia and the parliament of Canada is not a proper policy, then there is only-one of two courses open to him, either to abandon his views or to tender his resignation; and then, when he is a free man, when he has left the service and has ceased to draw his salary from the public chest, he would be free to say what he thinks, to criticise the action of the Minister of Militia or of any member of the government, or to criticise the military policy of Canada. He would be then free to go back to England and to say that he could not get on owing to political interference, and that he had tendered his resignation. But so long as this General Officer Commanding is in the position of any other public servant, he is bound to be silent, bound to do what would be the duty of any officer in his position in any- civilized country ; and I do not think that it is a well advised course on the part of the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) to come here and try to justify' the action of Lord Dundonald.

Does my hon friend mean to say that Lord Dundonald would be more justified after ceasing to be General Officer Commanding in attacking the government for its acts than he would be while he was General Officer Commanding and could take the responsibility of his acts ? I presume Lord Dundonald asks no favours, I presume he knows his business, and is quite ready to abide by the consequence of his acts ?

I think Lord Dundonald would be justified, once he handed in his resignation, in saying to the people of Canada, of Great Britain ahd of the empire, that the policy pursued by Canada in military matters is not a proper policy. Certainly when he is a free man, he is entitled to act as a free man; but I say he has not the right, being the deputy head of the militia of Canada, while in command of the militia having authority over the other soldiers, to give such an example of gross breach of discipline. It very ill became the hon. member to come here and take up the defence of Lord Dundonald as he has done today. Another General Officer Commanding thought that some officers, including the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) were not proper persons to give their views on military matters and wanted to lecture the hon. member for setting a bad example. Everything was then at issue according to the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes). The Governor General had to act, the government had to act, the parliament of Canada had to act in order to show that the hon. member for North Victoria should be free from the attacks of the military head of the militia of Canada.
I do not say that I disagreed with the hon. member for North Victoria. 1 never disagreed with him on that question. I think he was right in saying that General Hutton had not the right to attack him, a member

of parliament, and to say that Col. Hughes, member of parliament, should not speak in the parliament of Canada because he happened to be a colonel in the militia of Canada. If it was an improper thing for the General Officer Commanding to come in conflict with the liberty of a member of parliament who happens to be a member of the militia under the authority of the General Officer Commanding, what shall we say of the action of a General Officer Commanding who gives to the public opinions and criticisms of the man who is acting as responsible head of the department of which he is a servant? He criticised the action of his superior acting in his official capacity. Sir, I think it is sufficient to put the case in that light to show that whatever might be our opinions as far as Lord Dundonald personally is concerned, whatever might be our opinion even as to the policy of the government in military matters, it could not be suffered for five minutes that a public servant of the government of Canada, drawing pay from the people of Canada under the authority of the minister, should publicly criticise the gentleman who at the time was acting as minister of the department of which he is a servant. Therefore I think it should no longer be considered that this is the trial of the Minister of Agriculture. It is the trial of Lord Dundonald who has seen fit to bring before the parliament of Canada his case through the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes).

I think that hon. gentlemen opposite have lost sight of the fact-
