Mr. Speaker, refei'lng to tbe matter debated this afternoon, I join with my bon. friend tbe leader of tbe opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) in expressing tbe view that although tbe circumstance was regrettable from one point of view, yet, having regard to tbe fact that this will probably call public attention to tbe methods that have been prevailing in tbe past, in tbe end, it will be beneficial to the country. Heaving aside for tbe moment the fact that the hon. gentleman who occupies the responsible position of Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden) has confined himself very much to an explanation of the position of affairs without taking any very strong ground in the discussion, we have a trio of gentlemen, namely, the right hon. First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), the lion. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher), and the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bour-assa) attempting to justify this matter in all its different phases. I will devote myself for a moment or two to the most important of these gentlemen, and that is tbe right hon. tbe First Minister. Tbe right hon. gentleman tells us that lie quite agrees with the statements that have been made by more than one hon. gentleman who has spoken that this is a matter, probably above all other matters in connection with the government of Canada, which should be clear and fre^ of party politics.

The manner in which my right hon. friend proceeds to show that this is his belief is certainly somewhat singular. He points out that it is usual when anything is occurring in a riding to consult important personages in the riding and he particularly points out that it is customary to consult the member. Therefore he asks : Is the hon. Minister of Agriculture debarred from being consulted because he is Minister of Agriculture ?
In reference to that I say ' no ' if the position is for sale, and I say decidedly ' yes ' if we are to have decent methods prevailing in Canada. If we are to have, as is almost admittedly the case in reference to almost every other department of the public service, the sale of the different positions for the purpose of bolstering up the government and of consulting the interests of local politicians rather than the interests of the country, whether it is a matter of a public work or of the appointment of a judge or whatever it may be, if that method is also to be carried out in regard to the important question of selecting fit and proper persons to be officers in the various departments of the militia service of Canada, then, I say :	Yes, a fit and proper person
is the hon. Minister of Agriculture because it was in his territory that this new branch of the service was being created. He more than any other would know the local conditions and know as a matter of political expediency whether it was or was not in the interest of the party that a certain person whose name had been proposed should be appointed or not. It is very happily expressed in an independent Ottawa paper, the ' Evening Journal ' of to-day, which says :
. In this case especially, the district in which the regiment is raised, being the personal stamping ground of the Minister of Agriculture, a suspicion is not unreasonable until something more is known that the minister may be actuated by motives which have no connection with the militia service. I
I submit to the House, that, having regard to the utterances of the hon. Minister of Agriculture this afternoon and the evident bias he displayed, instead of freeing himself from that imputation, he has stamped indelibly on the minds of the hon. gentlemen who have heard him a very broad and definite suspicion that there are influences at work in this country which are not in the interest of the militia service. The right hon. gentleman also says, and in this he just echoes practically the language of the hon. Minister of Agriculture, that the hon. Minister of Agriculture represented that there were too many Conservatives among the officers named. That is exactly where the difficulty lies. The hon. Minister of Agriculture this afternoon, as has been said by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, in the very heated address he gave, establishes beyond all question
that the fact is that it was a party necessity, aye and a party prejudice that actuated the minister in bis determination to strike the name of Dr. Pickel from the list of officers presented by the commanding officer. It is not a question of too many soldiers, because, when it comes to sending our men out to the front to take the risk of losing their lives, of sacrificing their personal interests and of undergoing the hardships of warfare whether in South Africa or elsewhere, there is no discount upon Conservative soldiers. On any occasion we could not have too many of them. The proportion .could not be too large and I am exceedingly proud of the fact that on every occasion the percentage of Conservatives was overpoweringly large when they marched upon the field of battle in defence of the country and in defence of the empire.
But when it comes to a matter of what might be regarded as positions of emolument or honour, there may be too large a proportion of Conservative officers. In this idea the Prime Minister and Minis-, ter of Agriculture seem to be at one. I believe that on reflection, the Prime Minister will find that the speech he made this afternoon was, to say the least, injudicious. He told us that the chief cause of this trouble was that there was too large a proportion of Conservatives in the list of officers. I never understood until now. that when it came to the question of whether a man should serve his King or not, the question of Conservative or Liberal was ever raised. It is a national disgrace to Canada that it should be raised now. I regret the incident in one respect, although in another respect it may be well that it has haappened, should it bring about a better state of things. I regret that the Prime Minister and his Minister of Agriculture should plunge us into national disgrace by their definite announcement, that in the future the question of politics will enter into the selection of officers for the mi'.itia of Canada. I do not believe that there is any other country under the British Flag in which a responsible minister of the Crown would dare to make such a declaration. The First Minister was excited this afternoon ; he was in a fighting mood. He told us that he had been an officer once, although he did not indicate in what particular branch of the service, and I must say I never heard of the right hon. gentleman in that connection, although I do remember something about the banks of the Saskatchewan, but that has passed into ancient history. The right hon. gentleman told us, referring to Lord Dundonald, that he would not be dragooned b - any foreigner into assuming any position. When there was a protest from this side of the House against calling Lord Dundon-aid a foreigner, the right hon. gentleman took back the word, as he found he had

said more than was perhaps desirable. It is said that in what is in sober comes out drunk, and the truth slips out sometimes when a man allows himself to become excited. The substitution of the word ' stranger for the word ' foreigner ' did not greatly better the case. At all events I think I speak the sentiments of the Conservatives of Canada when I say, that in the case or this valiant British officer who has seen service for the empire in other parts of the world, who has added additional lustre to the great name he bears, when such a man comes amongst us, the Conservatives of Canada do not regard him as a stranger. We receive him as one of ourselves, and as a valiant defender to that great empire to which we all belong. As to the details of the case we are discussing, the Prime Minister told us that the chief officer in command had no local knowledge of the situation. Well, is is evidently because of the local knowledge and the local prejudices of the Minister of Agriculture, that we have been *led into this deplorable incident. It is bad enough to bring party politics into expenditure or public works but when it comes to introducing partyism into the question of who shall fight for the empire and for Canada, it is an unfortunate thing indeed. Let politics stop outside our volunteer force ; for God's sake don't import party politics when it comes to selecting men to defend the country. I contend that Mr. Fisher, with his local knowledge, and his local prejudices, was above all the least qualified to recommend these officers for positions. The Minister of Agriculture told us that Dr. Pickel was a strong political opponent of his, and unfortunately in this case, as in the case of the Auditor General and others, the party who tried the case was the man who was interested in the prosecution. It may be an accident, but it is peculiarly significant that the Minister of Agriculture at this particular juncture was taking the place of the Minister of Militia. The Prime Minister told us that it was the right of the cabinet council to scratch off such names as might be objected to. I am not at all sure of that. I am not up in military law, but the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes) read authorities which lead us to a different1 conclusion. When it comes to the cabinet or to the minister scratching the names of officers off the list approved by the General Officer Commanding because they are a little off colour in their political persuasion, I have no hesitation in saying that it is about the worst thing that could happen in the interest of the country. The Minister of Agriculture may be a high authority in aesthetic culture, he may be able to tell us as to the shades of a rose ; or as to something in the Oscar Wilde line, but when it comes to a question of robust soldiering,
I venture to say that he is the last man Mr. LENNOX.
to whom we would look for a correct judgement in that regard.
It must have been noticed by the House that the Minister of Agriculture got very angry this afternoon. There was enough to make him angry ; but I am glad that it did not make him any more formidable. I have noticed that some large men, when they are angry seem to become more formidable. It rather dwarfed the Minister of Agriculture. We had providence intervening on our behalf, and he really did not look any more dangerous than on other occasions. Now, I have a complaint to make of the Minister of Agriculture, and that is, that while he complains of the hon. member for North Victoria for having brought forward this question, and objects to the medium of communication between Lord Dun-donald and the House of Commons, yet he took the very unfair position, the position that reflects no credit upon him, of suppressing a portion of the truth and of refusing to give the whole truth to the House of Commons and through it to the people of Canada. When we reflect on what took place this afternoon-the repeated request of the hon. leader of the opposition that the document which was in the hands of the Minister of Militia should be given to the House ; when we know that although it was spoken of as a copy it was practically a duplicate of what came into the hands of the hon. member for Victoria ; and when we know what that document contained ; it is a very serious reflection upon the government-yes, upon the right hon. gentleman who leads the House, because it was at his instigation that it was refused. It is only of a piece with what we have had on many occasions, that is, that whenever these hon. gentlemen find that by going half way with a story, they can give it a different colouring, they absolutely refuse to divulge the information which will convey to the people the truth and the whole truth in regard to the matter. But I say the House and the people owe a debt of gratitude to the hon. member for North Victoria-I was going to say the minister, and no doubt he will be a minister sooner or later-for bringing this matter before the House ; otherwise we would not have had an adequate conception of what is the real truth of this ease. The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) objects particularly to the fact that a servant of the Crown should make a disclosure. I want to say that the hon. member has not exactly a correct conception of this matter. The officer of whom we are speaking is not a servant of the Crown so much as he is a servant of parliament and a distinguished servant of Canada for the time being ; and it is all-important, when issues arise between the administration and this officer, that the people should know exactly what is taking place between them. It is a case of concealment-a case of the government un-

fairly suppressing a portion of the facts. It is a case of the government having announced that they would deal with this matter to-day unfairly and dishonestly, retaining a portion of the facts, and refusing to give them to the House, it is a case of the hon. member for North Victoria coming to the rescue, and through the agency of the distinguished officer who has communicated the information, giving that information to the House and the country. I am glad indeed that we have by this means the opportunity of ascertaining what the exact facts are. Well, we have this trio-the First Minister, the Minister of Agriculture and the hon. member for Labelle-all uniting in a certain conclusion of the whole matter. The personal organ of the Minister of Agriculture has already dismissed the commanding officer. It points out that he must retire, that there is no alternative ; and the vicious, excited way in which the Minister of Agriculture spoke this afternoon leaves no question on our mind that so far as he is concerned he is determined that this official, who has forsooth had the temerity of opposing what he describes as a Minister of the Crown, meaning himself, shall certainly get his walking papers and be sent home. Whether that is the case or not-and I suspect that Lord Dundonald is not very particular in that regard-it has come to this, that the Chief Officer Commanding the militia of Canada cannot have a voice on a matter upon which he has formed an opinion, and upon which he alone, as distinguished from the Minister of Agriculture, is entitled to have an opinion. Whether this incident will result in Lord Dundonald retiring from connection with the militia of Canada or not, it will perhaps be a salutary lesson to gentlemen such as the Minister of Agriculture, that there is a limit beyond which they cannot swell themselves, and that they must remember that they cannot set the bounds entirely in regard to the selection of officers for the militia service. I am glad, therefore, that this matter has come up. We have a number of cases at the present time involving the issue as to whether certain officials or certain members of the cabinet shall have complete sway as against the best interests of the people. There is a united desire on the part of the three gentlemen whom I have named to get rid of this officer, just as there is a manifest desire to get rid of the Auditor General. But in both of these cases the people will be heard from, and we shall see whether the hon. gentlemen will not be obliged to withdraw from the exalted position they assume.

Mr. Speaker, I would not occupy the time of the House, even for the few moments that I intend to speak on this subject, were it not that I feel that it is one of the utmost importance to this country. We are to-day writing a
page of Canadian history which a few years, hence when hon. gentlemen opposite may be, on your left, and the hon. gentleman at your left may be on your right, they and this country may all wish had never been written. I hope it will not be thought presumptuous on my part if I venture to call the attention of the House to the fact that this afternoon, not only the Minister of Militia and the Minister of Agriculture, but even the right hon. gentleman who leads the House, appeared wholly to misconceive the question before us.
On listening to these hon. gentlemen, one would think that it is Lord Dundonald who is on trial before this House. But it must be evident to everybody who has followed the debate, that although the chief defendant has absented himself from court, and although his co-defendant fled even before him, still it is really the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Militia who are on trial here to-day. And when we consider the circumstances which have come to light, surely we are not to be blamed if we cannot help coming to the conclusion that the gentleman who is in command of His Majesty's forces in this country was not treated with proper respect by these ministers of the Crown. It would be difficult to come to any other conclusion even if we were to judge them solely by the contempt they show for this House in absenting themselves from this debate to-night. This afternoon again and again we heard it said-and I was sorry to hear the language used-that Lord Dundonald was a servant of the minister and a servant of the government. Surely no one seriously would contend that a gentleman in command of His Majesty's forces in Canada is a servant of either the Minister of Militia or the government. I would rather say that he is in the same position which the ministers themselves occupy-that he is peculiarly a servant of the people. And, Sir, it is a proud position to be a servant of the people. And if we admit that they are all servants of the people, then we, the representatives of the people, surely have something to say regarding the way in which they behave themselves ; and while I would be sorry to use any term which might be objectionable, I am more warranted in finding fault with the Ministers of Militia and Agriculture for their absence from the House, when their conduct is being discussed, than they were in their strictures upon General Lord Dundonald. In dealing with matters of which we can only know by hearsay, we may perhaps arrive at some accurate opinion if we view them in the light to be derived from the facts as they have been disclosed to-day. What are these facts ? A speech was made a week ago by Lord Dundonald in Montreal. Whether that speech was wisely made or not, it is not for me to say, but it was made, and I presume no one doubts that Lord Dundonald may be called on by the Minis-

It is very satisfactory to see that defenders of Lord Dundonald have not been wanting during the debate which has taken place this afternoon. It would have heen a pity indeed if a man occupying such a position as he occupied, with such a career as he has had, and with such services to his credit since he has been in Canada, should have had his case passed over with the mere personal explanation with which it was intended that it should be smothered this afternoon. I think it is a great pity that my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) should be absent fnom the House at a time when a discussion of this importance is taking place. For, in reality, under the motion that has been made by my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes) it is not the case of Lord Dundonald which we are discussing here, but it is the case of the Minister of Agriculture himself, who stands impugned, accused, before this House, of violating the most elementary principle of our Militia Law which requires that there shall be no political interference with the organization of our militia forces. Let me speak for the province of Quebec and from very reliable information whieh I have received. I am happy to say that, uniformly throughout that province, it has been recognized that, since his arrival in this country the General Officer Commanding, with a great deal of tact, a great deal of energy and a deep knowledge of the affairs he has been called upon to administer, has greatly improved the militia administration in the province of Quebec. He has improved the army service ; he has improved the Intelligence Department. He has many things in common with the French Canadians of my province ; he speaks their language fluently ; and from military men of that race in my province, I have heard it uniformly said that the

relations existing between him and them (have been generally satisfactory. Now, I do not wish to repeat what has already been said, but it seems to me that my right lion, friend the P#ime Minister has lost sight of an important aspect of the affair which should be stated. The ministers of the Crown occupy a dual position. As ministers, they themselves, are servants of the Crown. They are named by the Crown and their duties are defined by the statute-
They are responsible to the people.

Not as ministers as ministers they are responsible to nobody but the Crown. They are responsible to us as privy councillors, that is as constitutional advisers of the Crown. And it is just as illegal for the Minister of Agriculture to interfere with the administration of any of the departments of state except his own as it would be for me to interfere with the Department of Agriculture or any other. Of course that is a distinction that is recognized by all the authors who have written on constitutional law. It is a virtue of the custom of parliament that the constitutional advisers of the Crown happen at the same time to be ministers in charge of departments. It has not always been so. Less than a hundred years ago it was not so in England. But from the very fact of the introduction of constitutional government in England and of its subsequent introduction in this country, the custom has taken root which requires that those who, sis advisers of the Crown are responsible to parliament, should be those called upon by the Crown to take charge of the different departments of the state. I mention this fact because there seems to have been an impression, from some of the observations made this afternoon that it was quite legal and regular and constitutional for the minister in charge of one of the departments of state to go over into another department and order this or that to be done. And my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture himself, when he admitted to-day in his subsequent exp'anation-changing completely the facts of his first personal explanation -he seemed to think it was not only his right but his duty, long before the departure of the Minister of Militia, to interfere with the constitution of this regiment anu to see to it that it should be organized upon a proper basis, and the theory which my hon. friend the Prime Minister advocated when he spoke this afternoon was that, as a minister of the Crown, having charge of the Department of Agriculture, and with duties strictly circumscribed by 'laws passed toy parliament, the Minister of Agriculture still had the right, when the organization of this regiment was decided upon, to go to the Department of Militia, to have conferences Mr. MONK.
with the officers charged with the organization of that regiment and to interfere, to, in fact, take an important part himself in the organization of that regiment. X submit that by so doing the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) was clearly going beyond the limits placed upon his authority by parliament itself. This is a point of some importance, and I give a few words in explanation of it, because the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), who is a great deal fairer, I know, than he desires to appear to be, seems to have ignored that fact. If the House will take the trouble to refer to the statute creating the department of my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture and defining its limits, it will be found that parliament has strictly circumscribed the subjects upon which he can exercise jurisdiction. In section 2 of chapter 24 of the Revised .Statutes of 'Canada, section 4, I find the following :
The following subjects shall be under the control and direction of the Minister of Agriculture, that is to say, agriculture, immigration and emigration, public health and quarantine, the marine and immigrant hospital at Quebec, arts and manufactures, census, statistics and the registration of statistics, patents of invention, copyright, industrial designs and trade marks, experimental farm stations.
Beyond that my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture has no right of interference whatever. His authority is strictly circumscribed by parliament, and he has no more right to interfere with the Department of Militia, or with the organization of a regiment, than any other private citizen. Otherwise, if we were to adopt the theory of the right hon. gentleman, we would find that in reality every member of this House, conversant with the localities where regiments were to be organized, would have a right, as members of this House, to interfere and to control the organization of such regiments ; and what would that be but political interference and the introduction of politics into our military organization, a condition of affairs entirely undesirable in this country V
Now, let us for a moment leave the Department of Agriculture, and turn to the organization of the Department of Miilitia.
1 shall quote one or two sections in regard to this department, in order to show with what care parliament has determined and defined the duties of the Minister of Militia and the duties of the Officer Commanding, whose conduct has been, to a certain extent, under discussion this afternoon. The Department of Militia is organized under Chapter 41, Revised Statutes of Canada, and by section 4 of that statute it is enacted as (follows :
There shall be a Minister of Militia and Defence who shall be charged with and be responsible for the administration of militia affairs, including all matters involving ex-

penditure and of the fortifications, gun boats, ordnance, ammunition, arms, armouries, stores, munitions and habiliments of war belonging to Canada.
2.	The Minister of Militia and Defence shall have the initiative in all matters involving the expenditure of money.
3.	The Governor in Council shall, from time to time, make such orders as are necessary respecting the duties to be performed by the Minister of Militia and Defence.
Now, how are defined and how has parliament expressed itself in regard to the important functions of the General Officer Commanding ? We find that definition at section 37 of chapter 41, Revised Statutes of Canada:
There shall be appointed an officer who holds the rank of colonel or rank superior thereto in Her Majesty's regular army, who shall be charged, under the orders of Her Majesty, with the military command and discipline of the militia, and who, while he holds such appointment, shall have the rank of major general In the militia, and shall be paid at the rate of four thousand dollars per annum in full of all pay and allowances.
tinder the regulations provided for in this section it is stated of the General Officer :
He is the principal adviser of the Minister of Militia and Defence on all military questions ; is charged with the general supervision of the military branch of the department; issues general orders, and holds periodical inspections of the militia.
He is charged with the distribution, quartering and localization of the militia; With the preparation and maintenance of detailed plans for mobilization ; with the preparation of schemes for offensive and defensive operations ; and with the collection and compilation of military information.
He recommends to the Minister of Militia and Defence fit and proper persons for appointment to commissions in the militia ; and proposes fit and proper officers for promotion, for staff and other military appointments and for military honours and rewards.
It is sufficient to read chapter 41, creating and organizing the Militia Department, and the regulations governing the duties of the Minister of Militia and the General Officer Commanding to see that the will of parliament was that in the organization of regiments the approval of the nominations of all officers and of all promotions should ho carefully guarded by the General Officer Commanding. Had this discussion been left this afternoon with the general statement, the personal explanation of the Minister of Agriculture, what would have been the impression left upon the House and on the country V It would have been that the Minister of Agriculture at the instance of the Minister of Militia, absent for a short time, had merely performed a purely ministerial service to his colleague in initialling for him the list of these nominations. And what would have been the position before this House, before parliament, to whom all
ihese men are ultimately responsible, and before the country, of the General Officer Commanding ? It would have been that the statement made by him at a dinner given to him by his brother officers in regard to that most important branch of the administration of the state was a statement not founded on fact. It seems to me if the General Officer Commanding was aware that that was the turn which the proceedings in this House were going to take this afternoon, he should have put simultaneously into the hands of his superior, the Minister of Militia, and of my hon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes) *a man of military experience and with t military career, the memorandum which he did put in their hands, a memorandum which throws a very different compllexion on the whole subject. Is there or is there not truth in the statement, uncontradicted, but rather confirmed, by the Minister of Agriculture, that the organization of this regiment was determined upon early in the winter, in the month of February last ; that its organization was approved by the government and handed over to the officers who legally had charge of that organization? Ts it a fact that from the very inception the Minister of Agriculture interfered with that organization, blocked it and, for political purposes, as he admits this afternoon, endeavoured to organize the regiment himself and to Obtain the nomination of the principal officers of that regiment ?
It is impossible to refer to that very frank statement made by the colonel in command of the regiment to Lord Dundonald without being extremely surprised at the state of affairs revealed. Is it a fact that Dr. Pickel, whose nomination is here in question, was objected to for on other reason than that he was a strong political opponent of the hon. Minister of Agriculture ? Is it a fact that the hon. Minister of Agriculture was determined to block the whole organization unless Dr. Pickel's name was withdrawn V That has not been categorically contradicted by the hon. Minister of Agriculture and uncontradicted it gives us a clear explanation from the hon. gentleman of the reason that actuated Dr. Pickel, who, seeing that the regiment could not be organized unless he withdrew, which withdrawal was due to the unwarranted personal interference of the Minister of Agriculture authorized his name to be withdrawn. Is it a fact that the hon. Minister of Agriculture instead of confining his observations and remarks to the efficiency of the new regiment gave himself the trouble to look up the pedigrees and assure himself of the political affinities of the gentlemen whose names had been submitted to the hon. the Minister of Militia ? In face of these facts and the other facts stated in the letter evidently written by the colonel in defence of the position taken by the General Officer Commanding is it not a fair question for parliament and the mem-

bers of parliament to inquire if we are going to again this year vote a sum, as we are asked to vote, of over $2,000,000 for the organization of the militia which cannot be an effective militia, if, when regiments are organized, the only question inquired into is as to the political tendencies of the officers appointed ? I yield to no one in vindication of the rights and authority of this parliament. Nobody, as far as I have seen this afternoon, has called in question the right of the government to control the Department of Militia and Defence as it controls every other department, but I say this that I for one on behalf of my constituents will oppose any increase in the expenditure for militia purposes if we are going to have in the organization of our regiments such interference as has been admitted this afternoon by the lion. Minister of Agriculture. This is surely not a question of political division. I do not consider it is such. I am prepared as I am sure all other members of this parliament are prepared to vote the necessary sums to place the defence of this country upon such a basis as Will allow us to hold up our heads firmly and defend our country against any invader. But, at the same time, if we are to find in the constitution of any government men as unpatriotic, as unfair to the faithful servants of the Department of Militia and Defence, as the General Officer Commanding, it seems to me, has shown himself to be on this occasion, I say that we will be entitled to scrutinize with great care the expenditure which is foreshadowed to us in the estimates brought down to parliament this year.
As to the fact that the General Officer Commanding saw fit to make that statement which he did make at a dinner given to him by these officers, who, after all, may be called upon at any moment to stand the brunt of the fighting and to see to it that the forces which they organize are effective, it may be that he might have adopted some other form of communication, but if the provocation to which, since the month of February, the interference of the hon. Minister of Agriculture has subjected him to had been imposed upon myself I venture to say that I would have taken the first opportunity of freeing myeelf and my co-workers from the interference of a man who had nothing whatever, as minister to another department, to do with the administration of the Department of Militia and Defence.

that they look for the maintenance of the efficiency of that force and for the preservation of order and discipline in it. The attempt made by the hon. Minister of Agriculture this afternoon to defend himself from the allegations made at Montreal by Lord Dundonald has not been entirely successful. As has been pointed out, the hon. minister has frankly admitted that he has been interfering, and interfering to the detriment of the organization of the regiment in question, by objecting to the appointment of officers whose names were sent to him by the General Officer Commanding. He admitted frankly in the speech he made this afternoon that the name of Dr. Pickel was scored out because of his political affiliations.
The minister himself made that perfectly clear this afternoon. There were too many Tories being nominated for commissions from the district of Sweetsburg. The Minister of Agriculture, who was desirous that there should not be a semblance of politics in the administration of the force or in the organization of this regiment, thought that he knew more about the gentlemen who were being nominated to hold [commissions in this new corps than the colonel to whom was given the responsible task of organizing it, or of his superior Lord Dundonald who had endorsed his recommendations. And because there were two Tories nominated by those best calculated to judge, this hon. minister steps in and stamps his foot down vigorously and says the organization of this regiment will not be completed unless a change is made in the personnel of the officers. There were too many Tories in the 53rd Regiment, he said, and he must see to it that the error of having Tory officers is not repeated in the regiment we are about to organize. But what prevented the political friends of the hon. gentleman joining the 53rd Regiment ? Was there any barrier to their being admitted to commissions in the regiment at all ? If they are not to be found in the regulations of the militia, the hon. gentleman himself might give the reasons why.
I have.

There were no good reasons given, and the allegation that men were debarred from holding commissions in the militia force because of their political affiliations cannot be substantiated by the hon, gentleman.
It is true.

I regret that the hon. minister reiterates that statement, because I have known something of the militia force in my section of Ontario during many years, and I never knew of any time or occasion when any gentleman in the militia force, because of his political affiliations, was debarred or prevented from receiving pro-1485
motion or from being given a commission. Let me tell the hon. Minister of Militia that this is not the first time complaints have been made of the injury of the militia force by the promotion of political partisans by hon. gentlemen opposite. If this condition of things should continue, if the manly protest of Lord Dundonald does not produce the desired effect, grave danger will result to the force in the future. I have had pointed out to me an abuse in the organization of the army medical corps in the city of Toronto recently. The applications of men eminently qualified to hold positions in that corps, whose presence would be a guarantee of its fitness and excellence, were turned down, and political friends of hon. gentlemen opposite appointed because of pressure brought to bear on the Minister of Militia'.
Give the names.

I will give the hon, minister the names in private and will give him the opportunity of making a statement any time he sees fit respecting these names. I have nothing to conceal; but I am surprised that the Minister of Militia should have allowed such a condition of things to exist in connection with the establishment of this new regiment in the eastern townships, from which so much was to be expected. The testimony borne by hon. gentlemen opposite themselves as to the character and qualifications of Lord Dundonald to occupy the position he now holds is the strongest possible proof that can be adduced that all he is aiming at is the efficiency of our militia force. Has Lord Dundonald interfered in political matters ? Has he given any indication that he desires the appointment of officers in any regiment because of their political affiliations? None at all; but as my hon. friend (Mr. Northrup) has said, after having been repeatedly pin-pricked by gentlemen who ought to have known better, he became restive and felt it his duty to enter an emphatic protest, once for all, against such political interference, and to take such steps as he thought necessary to make the Canadian militia what we all desire it shall be. I shall not take up any more time except to enter an emphatic protest against the action of the hon. Minister of Agriculture. The statement made by Lord Dundonald and the protest he has entered will find a responsive echo in the breast of every man in Canada who has any regard for the militia force of this country, who desires to see it in a state of efficiency, removed altogether from the influence of party politics. Lord Dundonald is not an unknown man. He came here with an illustrious record. He had earned his spurs. He earned them long before he came to Canada. He is not a foreigner nor a stranger, Mr. Speaker. His name and his fame are known where-ever a man wears the British uni-

form, from one end to the other of this great empire, and his sole aim since he came here has been-and the Minister of Militia knows it as well as anybody-to promote the efficiency of our militia force, in whose welfare he has taken such a great interest. Is it because hon. gentlemen opposite feared that, becoming exasperated, the General Officer Commanding would enter his protest, they made provision in their new Militia Bill that in future the Genera! Officer Commanding may be a Canadian ? Have they found these sturdy Britishers who have been invited over here to command our forces not as pliable as they would like ? Have they found that these men would not allow the force to be degraded into a political machine ? Is that the reason we are to have this change made, so that those -who may command Our militia in the future will be men who will bow their heads meekly, and not stand up as men and soldiers should-as Lord Dundonald has done-in emphatic protest against a course which must be destructive of the best interests of the force and inimical to the best interests of Canada? I hope we shall never again, no matter what changes may take place in the force, witness an occurrence such as we have discussed in this House to-day. I repeat there was nothing else for Lord Dundonald to do than to let the people know what was going on in his department behind the scenes. There was nothing else for him but to let them know where the sore spot is. He, who was to be held responsible for the efficiency of the militia, was handicapped at every turn because the nominations made by his officers in the organization of a new regiment were being ignored and set aside solely on the ground that the persons nominated had the misfortune to differ in politics from the Minister of Agriculture. The picture is not a very happy one and does not reflect much credit on the Minister of Agriculture. There was nothing left for Lord Dundonald to do, under the circumstances, but make the speech he did, let the consequences be what they may.

As this unfortunate subject, Mr. Speaker, which has attracted the attention of the House this afternoon, seems to have originated in the section of country, from which I come, it will perhaps be not altogether_out of place that I should say something with regard to it.
The point has been raised this afternoon, and made a good deal of by the hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher), who, apparently, has been transformed into a fighting man fit to be head of the department of wat, decided that Dr. Pickel had not the qualifications to enable him to fill the position of officer in the reorganized mil-tia force of the district. Previous to this militia reorganization of this particular part of Mr. CLARKE.
the eastern townships, reorganization took place last year in the county which I have the honour to represent. The old 58tL battalion was reorganized as mounted infantry. The principle adopted in that case was that the colonel was called upon by the Department of Militia and Defence to reorganize or create a force of mounted rifles from the old 58th battalion of infantry that had existed in the county for many years. As I understand it, the colonel was given carte blanche to select his officers, irrespec tive of whether they had passed any examination or not. Mr. Speaker, I am not versed in military matters, and do not pretend to have any knowledge of the details of this -reorganization. It not being a political matter, so far as the county I represented was concerned, I took no particular interest other than to give such indirect assistance as I could by communicating, as representative of the county, with the Department of Militia at the instance of those interested. The reorganization took place. Young men were selected for their worth as citizens first. Though not pretending to know anything about militia matters, I believe that the upright, honest, straightforward, patriotic young citizen is the best foundation for a soldier you can find. They were selected on that ground. The officers of that reorganized corps had not passed their examination. The Minister of Militia was good enough to establish a school at Sherbrooke in the autumn after the first year of their drill, and in that school these officers became qualified, and this year they are going out full qualified men after having passed the requisite examination. Under these cir cumstances, I think that the argument presented to this House by the Minister bf Agriculture that Dr. Pickel was not qualified falls to the ground. In the case I referred to, we had an entire regiment, or whatever they choose to call it, reorganized with officers who had not the necessary qualifications. So far as Dr. Pickel is concerned, I am not here to defend him ; and. if he were present, it would not be neeessarv for any man here to rise in his defence, for he is quite capable of defending himself anywhere. He is very popular, a man of splendid character and of precisely the right age. And, as I understand it and know the facts, when the reorganization of this imilitia force in the county of Missisquoi was proposed they were looking for a man of character, some natural leader of men, to take i prominent position in the militia force and make the organization absolutely -successful -not to make it, as the Minister of Agricul ture said this afternoon, a political machine ; not at all ; but to make it what the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) and every other good citizen of Canada would desire, as perfect a militia organization as it was possible to get in that vicinity. In order to accomplish that Dr. Pickel was soqght. He did not seek the positon ; he is

beyond seeking positions ; positions are offered to him. The people who know him best offer him the best it is in their power to give him. Those interested in this reorganization sought him and asked him to fill this positicn. He accepted it with modesty ; lie felt that he was not a qualified officer, and made certain excuses on that ground. But finally he said : I am a good, loyal citizen of Canada, and if my connection-temporary, if nothing else-will do something to help the reorganization of this militia force and put it on a proper footing,
I consent. These were the conditions under which he consented. And we can readily understand that, when it was represented to him that his connection with the force, from the very fact that he was a prominent Conservative, was checking the work of reorganization, he would say at once : I do not want it ; it is nothing to me ; put me out and go on with the reorganization, if it will please the Minister of Agriculture and help on the work, leave me out. Every one who knows Dr. Pickel knows that that is the way he would regard it, and the Minister ot Agriculture knows it perfectly well. So far ns the family history in connection with Senator Baker, or with any other Conservative family of the eastern townships, that the Minister of Agriculture has presented here to-day, I do not think it is altogether a ground of fault-finding for those Conservative families to say that they are built of the peculiar stuff of loyalty and patriotism that, when you want to form a militia corps, you are obliged to go to a Conservative family to find the leaders, the men in whom the rank and file will have confidence. It may suit the purposes to-day of the Minister of Agriculture. I listened to that hon. gentleman-of course, I speak under prejudice ; T understand that perfectly well ; I own the corn, I speak under prejudice. At the same time I listened to the speeches the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fisher) delivered. At first I remarked the articles that had been prepared and typewritten for him and that he read ; and then I listened to his second speech, in which he contradicted every position taken in those typewritten articles, and in which he confessed the crime-if it is a crime-with which he is charged. If it is a crime for a public man in a high position, moved by influences which do not appear on the surface, to prefer one citizen as against another as a defender of this country, then the Minister of Agriculture is as guilty as any criminal who ever stood in the dock, and that is proven toy his own confession in this House. Now, the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) made a speech this afternoon. He insisted that the General Officer Commanding should understand that the government of this country would not be dragooned. Yesterday we had a statement from'one of the right hon. gentleman's lieutenants in the Senate. And, putting these two things together, we have the principle
laid down by the Prime Minister that if the General Officer Commanding chose to do anything for the militia of Canada without consulting the Privy Council he would be guilty of dragooning the government.
The right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) also said that in his early days he was a military man.
I was surprised to hear that. We knew there was a period in his life when he expressed a willingness to be a soldier. We knew that he had said that he would shoulder his musket on the banks of the Saskatchewan to fight on behalf of a rebel. That is the only time I ever heard of the right hon. gentleman shooting a gun in the Dominion of Canada. I do not know if he refers to an earlier part of his career, there may be an earlier part when the right hon. gentleman was unknown to Canada. But, Sir, he is not the only soldier. We have another soldier in the rank of the government, the Minister of Agriculture. It may not be known to you Sir, but I shall inform you in order that you may carry it back to the constituencies in which you commune now and again. The Minister of Agriculture is a gallant officer. True he has never passed any examination, true he has never fought any battle for his country true he has never substantiated any principle that he ever fought upon. But nevertheless he is 'supposed to be a gallant soldier.	He found, perhaps for
the benefit of his health, perhaps because he had been promoted to a high position as a member of this government, and become to some extent an aristocrat, that it was incumbent upon him to own a saddle horse, and he bought one. This horse was not easy to ride, and you can understand as well as I can that a man who has toiled hard and long upon, the farm, pulling *weeds and hoeing corn and digging away and spreading manure, is not suited to a horse that is not docile and to a certain extent cumbersome. It was suggested to the gentleman who was keeping the livery stable in this city that exercise might be given to this horse, and he went to the Minister of Agriculture. It was intimated to him that the volunteers were about to go forth to their annual drill and that somebody might be induced to ride this horse and pay him for its use and, being a great financier, as well as a patriot and a man of war, he determined that his horse should serve his country which he had never done, and that he should get paid for its use. The double temptation was great, and the horse went forth to battle. He battled for 12 days which is the rule in this country and fought those imaginary battles that are fought under these conditions, and then he returned. As you know the volunteer, the man who leaves his business and goes forth into these imaginary battles receives for himself and his horse $1.50 a day, and if you multiply that by 12, you will find that

he gets $18 altogether. That is what the man got for the horse belonging to the Minister of Agriculture and himself for those 12 days. Now, Sir, it is the Minister of War we are speaking of, and to show his deep patriotism, his intense interest, as he portrayed it this afternoon, in the development of the militia system of Canada-I was surprised to hear him as I did not know that he possessed such intense interest and patriotism-the generosity of that Minister of War or that pro-Minister of War was so great that when this man came to him with that $18, which he had received for himself and the horse, the Minister of War took the whole $18. We do not often get such sacrifice, such evidence of deep patriotism, such soldierly feeling, perhaps in the empire, not alone in Canada. When I heard the minister to-day and saw him standing with defiance and saying that he assumed the entire responsibility in this matter, although we have had some humorous and ridiculous situations, I do not think we have ever seen anything as funny as the valiant position taken by the proMinister of War. Of course there were no guns pointed towards him and he was absolutely safe when fighting this great battle. Sir, a man who had taken $18 for the use of a horse for 12 days when the poor devil only got $18, could not stoop to any position other than the most honourable, and when I heard him I said to myself : At last that animosity, that miserable feeling which I should not entertain towards the Minister of Agriculture must vanish, and when I go forth from this House I must bow with that great respect that should be given by every citizen of Canada when he meets a man moved with these deep, manly, warlike feelings, which the Minister of Agriculture is supposed to entertain.
The representative of the Prime Minister in the Senate yesterday said that the General Officer was to be a servant of Canada. We are all servants of Canada' and the true servant is the man who does bis work without prejudice. I have heard that the general has not brought this question before the House with a lawyer's dexterity. That is the absolute test of his honesty as a soldier ; let it come here as it might. It is said that he gave the memorandum to the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) when he should have given it to the minister. When was that presented- to this House ? After the clock pointed to the hour of three. The master owes a duty to the servant as well as the servant to the master, and it is the duty of the master to protect the servant until be does not deserve protection. I ask whether that servant had not the right to expect a letter, a request from the minister to go to his office in order to discuss this situation, to see if he had any defence for the position he took in Montreal. He waited until three o'clock. Would you ask him to Mr. POPE.
wait until four ? Was he to go to the master who had said nothing to him, or was he to present to parliament his simple defence and let parliament decide on its merits ? I believe the general took the right course. We are all servants, the Prime Minister is a servant, the President of the United States is a servant, the King of England is a servant if you like. Do you, Mr. Speaker, or the right hon. Prime Minister or any member of the government tell me that because the King of England receives a salary, that because the President of the United States receives a salary, or that because the Prime Minister receives a salary, there is to be no distinction between any of these, and the most menial servant who labours in this country ? Has the time arrived when no distinction is to be made ? I say that the King of England has a right to be treated according to the position which he occupies, that the President of the United States has the right to be treated according to the position which he occupies, and the right hon. Prime Minister according to the position that he occupies, and I say that the General Officer Commanding who stands at the head of the militia force of Canada, has the right to the same treatment and not to the treatment of the most menial servant in the land.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that perhaps the most regrettable thing in connection with thisj question is the fact that a responsible minister of the Crown and a man who, entertains a very high opinion of the prerogatives and privileges of a minister of the Crown should stand up in this House and in the presence of the commons of Canada make a statement in reference to a matter of this kind such as the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) has made this afternoon, a statement, Sir, which before he got through, he was obliged to contradict when he found that there was in possession of an hon. member on this side of the House, a memorandum setting forth the case which contained a clear, distinct and absolute refutation of the statement which the hon. minister had made in his first, prepared and typewritten remarks. I say, Sir, that the conduct of the hon. Minister of Agriculture is a humiliaton not only to himself but a humiliation to the government of which he is a member, and a humiliation to this parliament. It is astonishing that an hon. minister of the Crown, or a supposedly hon. minister, would attempt to misrepresent the facts to the members of this House. In the typewritten statement which the hon. minister read this afternoon to us he claimed to be actuated only by a desire that the portion of the militia force situated in the eastern townships that was being reorganized should be reorganized in the best possible manner and that he was purely and

absolutely concerned in seeing that th^ interests of the militia force were safeguarded. But, before he got through his verbal statement, he made it plain that he was actuated by a desire to introduce politics into the militia of that part of the country and see to it that Conservatives were not appointed to positions of honour in that regiment. Now, Sir, I regret that the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Frederick Borden) has been compelled by force of circumstances to lower himself in the estimation of the country, for I do consider that he has lowered himself and that he has lowered the position which he occupies in the country. He has been looked upon as a very good Minister of Militia, as good a Minister of Militia as a Liberal could possibly be. But, I am afraid that as a result of the line he has taken to-day he will shrink considerably and that bis glory will become considerably lessened in the eyes of the people of Canada. We find that the names of sixteen persons were recommended for appointment as officers of this regiment. Of these persons only two, Major D. W. Stewart and Captain G. Carr, were qualified according to the militia regulations for the positions to which they were appointed. In fact, the very man who was put in the place of Dr. Pickel was not a qualified officer under the militia rules. So that the only argument which the hon. minister or the Minister of Agriculture could possibly bring forward to justify the striking out of the name of Dr. Pickel is the fact that he is a Conservative. Lord Dundonald, the ablest, the best and the most popular Commander-inChief that Canada ever had is to have his head struck off merely from the desire of the Minister of Agriculture to introduce politics into the militia. No Tory need apply i-that is written on the door of the Militia Department. Perhaps if the general had been a little more yielding, a little more pliant, a little more submissive in his intercourse with the Minister of Agriculture, perhaps if he had been able to realize a little tin god when he saw one he would not have had as much difficulty with the hon. minister as he had. But, in his innocence, he had the temerity to use the telephone with that high and mighty personage, the hon. the Minister of Agriculture. He communicated with the hon. minister by telephone. He attempted to discuss this matter with him, but so great a man as the Minister of Agriculture, this expert on chicken fattening, was not to be treated in such a cavalier manner as to be talked to over the telephone. This great man, this minister must be approached in a more servile, a more submissive manner, because he resents the attempt of the Commander-in-Chief to talk to him over the telephone. We have had some striking differences of opinion as to
what has occurred in connection with this matter. We have had such wide divergences of statement that somebody must be telling what is untrue. In plain language somebody must be lying. Who is it ? Is it the general, Lord Dundonald, because the statement of Lord Dundonald in respect to what took place between himself and the hon. minister does not coincide with the statement of the hon. Minister of Agriculture. The divergence is so great and the points of divergence are so essential that it is impossible that it is a mere matter of mistake. The statements of the hon. Minister of Agriculture and Ool. Smart do not coincide. There is the same wide divergence, the same variance between their statements as there is between the statement of the hon. minister and Lord Dundonald. Ool. Smart has no prejudice in this matter as far as I can understand. I believe that Col. Smart is of the same political complexion, at least I have understood so, although I have not the honour of the acquaintance of that gentleman, as has the hon. minister. Ool. Whitley who is the brigadier of the district is of the same political eom-plection. Whatever object they would have in changing or colouring would be to do so on behalf of the Minister of Agriculture. But, they are honest, truthful men. We have the statement of Col. Whitley. The statement of Ool. Smart is an entirely different and distinct statement from that of the hon. Minister of Agriculture. He says in this letter of May 19, that Dr. Pickel was induced to consent to the withdrawal of the recommendation that had been made and as my hon. friend from Compton (Mr. Pope) said that very consent reflects the highest credit and honour upon Dr. Pickel, because if there were no other evidence in the case, that would stamp him as a man of such honour and integrity as would convince any non-partisan person that he would be a most excellent man to have in the militia of Canada. Whom are we to believe ? Are we to believe the statement of the hon. Minister of Agriculture which is absolutely contradictory in itself or are we to believe the statement of those three gentlemen who have no object whatever in misstating or misrepresenting the facts.
It seems to me that apart from any question of political partisanship we must of necessity believe the statements of two honourable men like Lord Dundonald and Col. Smart. That being so, what sort of an opinion are we to form of the Minister of Agriculture who would so far forget his ministerial position-of which he seems jealous enough when it comes to a question of precedence-what sort of opinion are we to have respecting such a man ; what sort of opinion can the country or even his own supporters have respecting him, when he can get up in this House as he did, and make a statement with the sole intention

of misleading lion, members* and misleading the people of this country. It has been said that Lord Dundonald was guilt}" of a grave breech of etiquette, if not discipline, in placing that memo, in the hands of the member for North Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes). Let us see how fair the government have been to Lord Dundonald. Yesterday, the Prime Minister announced that the matter would be taken up to-day, and from that hour to the present no communication, so far as we have been informed, has passed between the Minister of Militia and Lord Dundonald. There has been no request to Lord Dundonald to give his side of the case. If the members of the government had, been honest, if they desired to be fair to General Dundonald, the Minister of Militia would have read General Dun-donald's statement when he was asked to do so. Nay, he would not have waited to have been asked. If the Minister of Militia were a fair man and desired to do justice and fair-play to the gentleman who is claimed, to be an officer of his department; he would not have waited to be asked to read that memorandum, but in connection with his own presentation of the case he would have presented Lord Dundonald's side too. But Lord Dundonald knew well the class of men he was dealing with ; he knew well how little dependence was to be placed on their sense of justice, and consequently, in order to protect himself, he placed in the hands of my hon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes) a memo, which at the same time he sent to the Minister of Militia. Why, Sir, in the conduct of a trial, when the plaintiff's attorney states His case to the jury, he also states the pleadings on the other side. Lawyers are not generally supposed to be fair to their opponents, but, Sir, the fairness of lawyers shines out in contrast to the manner in which the Minister of Militia and the Minister of Agriculture have treated Lord Dundonald in this affair. Sir, this seems to me as a most regrettable incident, regrettable because of the unworthy conduct-I hope I am not unparliamentary-Mr. Speaker shakes his head.

That means that you are parliamentary.

speechtext: I do not think the hon. gentleman means to say that, because it would be unparliamentary.

Then, Mr. Speaker, we will consider it not said ; we will let the meaning go just the same. I was somewhat surprised at the statement which fell from the lips of the Prime Minister to-day. Is it to be said by the Prime Minister of a British colony, that a man of British birth and of British parentage, when he comes * to a colony of Great Britain, is a foreigner. The Prime Minister when he used the word Mr. FOWLER.
saw that he made a great mistake. A man who had shed his blood for this great empire ; a man whose ancestors for many generations back have fought and bled to the upbuilding of this great empire of ours ; such a man to be characterised by the Prime Minister of a British colony as a foreigner
Oh.

Who says oh ? I can quite understand a remark of that kind coming from an _ hon. gentleman opposite. I have heard the words the Prime Minister has uttered. I can understand something of the feeling that actuates him towards British generals and British officers ; but, Sir, thank God, that feeling is not widespread throughout this Dominion of Canada. The Prime Minister amended the Word ' foreigner,' by calling the General Officer Commanding a stranger. Dundonald, the man whose name is a household world throughout Canada, to be caHed a stranger in Canada. The amendment jyas very little better than the original in the mouth of the Prime Minister. No, Mr. Speaker, Lord Dundonald is neither a stranger hor a foreigner on any soil where the British flag floats. Now, the Minister of Agriculture expressed a great desire that a certain lieutenant who had been in South Africa and who had won the V. C. should be an officer in this regiment. That was right. I believe promotion should go to the most deserving, and that the men who have gone in active service to fight for their country should have a share of the honours. But tiie Minister of Agriculture and his friends were not always so favourable to that idea. When the coronation of the King was about to take place ip London, there was a little junketing trip for some members of the militia of Canada. The Minister of Militia and the government were not so solicitous then that the men who fought in South Africa should be placed on the coronation contingent. We moved from this side of the House, that such men should be given the preference, but it did not suit the purpose of the government, and they voted our motion down. But now it suits the minister of Agriculture to tell another story, and he says that he was actuated by a desire that this lieutenant who had gallantly won the Victoria Cross should be an officer of that regiment. This lieutenant was and is upon the force, and it was not necessary that he should take the place of Dr. Pickel; there were other vacancies to which he could be appointed. But, any port in a storm ; any excuse will suit the Minister of Agriculture when an excuse is hard to find. So far as I am concerned I am not actuated by any desire to make political capital out of this regrettable thing. I am desirous, as are all the members on this side of the House, for the welfare of the milita of Canada. I was at one time coni

nected with our militia, and I am anxious indeed that nothing should be done to injure the efficiency of the force upon which we have to depend in case of difficulty with our neighbours to the south, or with any other nation. I regret exceedingly that the usefulness of a man like General Dundon-ald-the best and most efficient Commander-in-chief we ever had in Canada-should be cut short by the conduct-the narrow-minded. bigoted conduct of the Minister of Agriculture. That is what I characterize it.
I can characterize his conduct in no other terms that could properly fit it, and I submit with confidence that these terms are not unparliamentary. I say that the narrow and bigoted, politically bigoted conduct of the Minister of Agriculture, will have a most serious effect if the result be, that we are to lose the services of General Lord Dundonald to the militia of Canada.
I presume, Mr. Speaker, that you will accord me the right of closing the debate, unless some gentleman on the other side wishes to speak.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit me to say, lest there be any misunderstanding, that in the view of the government the question before the House to-day is not the propriety of Lord Dun-donald's conduct. That is a separate question. The course of the discussion to-day has perhaps inevitably taken the form of personal explanations by the Minister of Militia and the Minister of Agriculture. In the view of the government, the question of the propriety of Lord Dundonald's course is a different matter, and we have purposely refrained from discussing it to-day. It will come up in due course. I merely wish to make this explanation.

The hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), in his remarks, seemed to take for granted that the general officers sent here by England had never realized any responsibility 'to the government of the country. While that may hay* been true in the case of some former General Officers Commanding, it has yet to be shown where Lord Dundonald has been anything else than thoroughly constitutional. The Minister of Militia, thank heaven, is the oniy minister to whom the General Officer Commanding owes allegiance. Let it be understood that no General Officer Commanding, and no other military officer of this country, has to pay allegiance to any Minister of Agriculture, be he never so small or never so great. Lord Dundonald has never yet been charged with being unconstitutional or with failing to recognize to the fullest extent his responsibility to the Minister of Militia. Lord Dundonald has ever been considerate in his dealings with the officers and men with whom he has been associated in Canada. He recognizes to the fullest extent his allegiance to the Minister
of Militia and the powers, of parliament in relation to the militia of this country. He has never sought to override his minister by claiming that he had a right to approach in his official capacity the Governor General of Canada. And, Sir, Lord Dundonald has never yet been insubordinate to his minister. 1 have watched .his career very carefully ; and when hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House sought, in reference to a speech which he made some time ago in Hamilton, to make it appear that he had been guilty of insubordination, his minister never admitted the charge. But there are times when patience ceases to be a virtue ; and, as my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) has said, the pin pricking of the Minister of Agriculture, not merely during the two or three days that he was acting Minister of Militia, but for many weeks, since last February, all through the months of March, April, and May, and even into the month of June, Lord Dundonald has borne with a great dekl of .patience. There is a feeling abroad-it was displayed by the Minister of Agriculture on this occasion- that the position of the General Officer Commanding in Canada, because he happens to be an imperial officer, is one of servitude. Let these hon. gentlemen disabuse themselves of any such notion. By accepting service in this country, in the position of General Officer Commanding' neither Lord Dundonald nor any other officer occupies a position of servitude to these people, and is not to be insulted and taunted and thwarted and belittled on every occasion. lhey may just as well realize once for all that the people of this country are not going tamely to submit to their petty tyranny in order to drive these officers out of the country. However, we shall have that discussed later on. The Minister of Agriculture did me the honour to refer to flay having a position on the staff bf this country, and he criticised Lord Dundonald for sending to me the communication which was presented to this House to-day, instead of sending it to the Minister of Militia. It has been pointed out, Sir, by more than one hon. member on this side of the House, as well as by hon. gentlemen on tne other side, that Lord Dundonald was not called on by the government for any statement here to-day. Had the bald statement of the Minister of Agriculture, supplemented by the statement of the Minister of Militia, gone to the country im the way in which it was read by him to this House to-day, I leave it to this House and the country if a false impression-if I am parliamentary I will say a deliberately false impression- would not have been conveyed to the people of this country. That was only prevented by the fact that yesterday, when the First Minister announced that he was going to bring this matter up to-day, and when he declined my request to have it postponed till Monday, I wondered what the other side

of the case might be. As I have already stated, I have in m.y desk letters on this matter from honourable citizens of the Eastern Townships ; but I wrote a letter and sent it to Lord Dundonald, asking him if I might have an interview with him or have some statement from him on this subject ; and at ten minutes after three to-day that statement was re'ad by me for the first time. I presume that His Lordship waited until the last minute to get a request from his minister or from the government, in order that he might have his case presented to the country side by side with that of the Minister of Agriculture. But, true to the spirit of unfair play which lias characterized the hon. Minister of Agriculture in the past, and which has characterized him in the present instance, the General Officer Commanding would have been given no opportunity to have his case presented to the people of Canada and the empire at large had I not taken the course X did ; and the bald statement of the Minister of Agriculture would have gone before the people of Canada and the empire, and would have been in itself deceiving. The Minister of Agriculture referred to my position on the staff, and implied that Bord Dundonald had demeaned himself by addressing a letter to one who occupies a position on the staff. As I pointed out to-day, as a member of parliament 1 am absolutely independent. That question has been fought out by me before this. 1 had the honour of educating the Minister of Militia, and he knows it. I had the honour of educating the .Prime Minister, and he knows it. I have not yet taken the Minister of Agriculture in hand. I may before the end of the session
