HUGHES-and if I tackle him, he will be educated-let him make no mistake. He will be a sadder and a wiser man when I am through with him. I had the honour of educating these gentlemen some years ago on their duties in relation to members of parliament holding positions in the militia service of the country. A member of parliament owes allegiance to no superior ; the people alone are his masters, and these gentlemen may just as well understand it.
I have had the honour of being offered the highest civil service position in the militia of this country. Many years ago I was offered the position now held by Colonel Piriault-that of deputy Minister of Militia; but I had seen a former deputy Minister of Militia, a former adjutant general, treated by members of the Liberal party before committees of this House worse than slaves were ever treated. And i made up my mind that if I became a civil servant, to be treated as those gentlemen were, there was only one way to teach them their duty and that was oy Mr. SAM. HUGHES.
appealing to them through the hide. I determined therefore that I would always be in a position to treat those gentlemen as they deserved without violating my duty as a servant of the country. Accordingly, neither did I accept long years ago the offer of the position of Deputy Minister of Militia, nor did I later in 1894 accept the position of Adjutant-General of Canada. * I declined to be a civil servant in this country. The hon. Minister of Agriculture had had the brazen hardihood to stand up in this House and tell us how he did interfere in the appointments of officers to this regiment and had struck off the names of Conservatives. Let me tell him that I had the honour of commanding a regiment a good many years and that I am in the service thirty-seven years. I had an officer who had risen from the ranks to a captaincy, and had been in my regiment some fifteen years, and I never knew until this spring that he was a member of the Liberal party. I only knew it when in conversation one day he told me himself. Neither directly nor indirectly have I ever, as the best officers in the regiment can testify, permitted politics to interfere in my conduct of its affairs. Liberals as well as Conservatives can bear testimony to that statement ; and although I am now out of the regiment, my hon. friend will find that the officers who served under me and the men also are to-day staunch supporters of mine simply because I have always treated them as men and not as politicians. I wish to emphasize this aspect of the case to the First Minister. As pointed out by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), the Minister of Agriculture has been guilty, I shall not say of treason, but of very improper conduct, and if the right hon. gentleman does not dismiss his colleague from the cabinet, he will be recreant in his duty to the Canadian people. .The question has been asked by the same Minister of Agriculture why there were so few Liberals in the corps. I need hardly tell the hon. gentleman that the policy pursued by the Liberal party during many years has not been such as to induce Liberals to wear uniforms of His Majesty and come to the defence of their country. The policy of the Liberal party would lead us to come under the Stars and Stripes. Their policy during many years tended towards annexation and was no encouragement to young Liberals to fan in and wear the uniform of men determined to uphold British institutions. It is the teaching of the hon. gentleman and his colleagues which accounts for so many of our young Liberals not being found in the force. However, I am proud to say that they have torn themselves away from these gentlemen and are now coming into the force in large numbers. Just one more reference to the hon. Minister. It was not Lord Dundonald-as the First Minister has attempted to point out-who selected these

officers, but Col. Smart who, I am told, is a Liberal, and Col. Whitley and Col. Roy, all Liberals. These are the three who were selecting officers for the regiment and who had to approve of these officers before sending in their names to the General Officer Commanding. They had no interests to serve other than the best interests of the regiment. But the Minister of Agriculture was not content to accept their selections, and sought to gratify his petty spite and prejudices by keeping good and efficient men out of the service. Another statement of the First Minister was this. He referred to Lord Dundonald as a foreigner and a stranger. Let me tell the right hon. gentleman that Lord Dundonald is a Britisher and so are all Canadians, irrespective of language, race or nationality. We are all Britishers, Sir, and mark you we intend to remain Britishers. It was Britain which won, has held, has upbuilt and has peopled this country, and let me tell the right hon. the First Minister that we intend it shall remain British. It shall not be annexed to the United States. It shall not become independent of Britain, because the people who never hesitated to come to the front in times of necessity have decided that it will remain British if they know their business. Let me tell you, Sir, further that Canadians owe allegiance first to the empire of which Canada forms a part, and that they intend remaining British; and should the time ever arrive when any Canadian government will demand the allegiance of Canadians to an independent Canada on the one hand in preference to the old empire, including Canada, on the other, the rebel will be he who declines to stand by the old British empire. I think, judging by the general conduct of these gentlemen, that the time has arrived when we may as well lay down the law to them ; and if the time should ever come when these hon. gentlemen will undertake to bring about such a condition of affairs as they would lead us to believe they have in view, they will find that they will have to depend not on horses alone and that it will require some thing more than horses to accomplish what they desire. Let me tell the right hon. the First Minister furthermore that Lord Dundonald is no foreigner and no stranger in this Dominion.
